tier_reason: First-party README states 'It consistently beats IndexedDB performance up to 10x' with read (SELECT SUM) and bulk-insert charts as images, measured on a 2015 MacBook Pro in Chrome; the benchmark code is public (src/examples/bench: queries.js, queries-raw-idb.js, main.worker.js) but CPU model, browser version and the charted values are not given in text, so not A, and no independent measurement was reachable, so not B.

corrections.caveats: First-party only; the headline 'up to 10x' is the only number in text, and the chart images (user-images.githubusercontent.com) could not be opened here, so per-test values were not read. Hardware is a 2015 MacBook Pro with no CPU model; Chrome version not stated. Baseline harness (src/examples/bench/queries-raw-idb.js) is the slowest raw-IndexedDB pattern: sumAll walks an openCursor one record per step and populate issues one store.put per row, while absurd-sql packs rows into 4096-byte SQLite blocks; Nolan Lawson's follow-up post 'Speeding up IndexedDB reads and writes' (2021-08-22) argued batched getAll()/getAllKeys() pagination and relaxed durability close much of that gap (search snippet only: in Chrome a 50,000-row cursor read took 1194.2 vs 488.3 with 1,000-item batches, units not shown). Timing is asymmetric: the SQLite sumAll timer starts after db.prepare, the raw-IDB timer includes opening the transaction. The harness's populateLarge inserts 400,000 rows. Requires the author's sql.js fork (@jlongster/sql.js), SharedArrayBuffer with COOP/COEP headers, and a worker; Hackaday's write-up (snippet only) says native SQLite is 2-3x faster than absurd-sql. This is a storage-layer win over the IndexedDB API, not a wasm compute win. Last commit 2023-08-06 (a merged @actualbudget patch); abandoned.

notes: README claim and benchmark code confirmed; record accurate at C. Shortcomings: baseline uses one-record IDB cursors and per-row puts instead of batched getAll (independent critique by Nolan Lawson, snippet only), chart values unreadable, no CPU model or browser version, abandoned since 2023.

tier_reason: No numbers were found anywhere reachable: the TISMIR 2021 paper (doi 10.5334/tismir.111), the UPF repository copy and the publisher mirror were all DNS-blocked here, search snippets give only the benchmark setup (two browsers, Node.js, four devices, vs native Essentia and Meyda) and not the results or their direction, and the MTG/essentia.js-benchmarks harness repo publishes no results. With benchmark_url null and no numbers page found, the record cannot stay above D.

corrections.claimed_speedup: No numbers seen. The TISMIR 2021 paper (Correya et al., doi 10.5334/tismir.111) and the ISMIR 2020 paper benchmark Essentia.js against native Essentia and the Meyda JS library (two browsers, Node.js, four devices including Android and iOS, per search snippets), but the results, and whether Essentia.js was faster than Meyda, could not be read.
corrections.caveats: Lead only: no speedup figure or direction of result was verified; a verifier with paper access should read the TISMIR results section. Benchmark harness lives in MTG/essentia.js-benchmarks (AGPL-3.0, 7 stars, last commit 2021-09-02): node/benchmark/*.js run benchmark.js suites 'Meyda#X' vs 'Essentia#X' over 24 algorithms, python/ runs pytest-benchmark on native Essentia; no results files are committed. Harness flaws seen in node/benchmark/MFCC.js and index.js: both paths are fed the raw WAV file bytes from fs.readFile (header included, never decoded to float samples), the two paths do different per-frame work (Meyda slices and re-sets bufferSize per frame, Essentia adds explicit Windowing), and index.js forks all 24 benchmark scripts at once so they contend for CPU; whether the paper used this runner is unknown. Main repo has no benchmark directory; last commit 2022-07-19, abandoned.

notes: Downgrade C to D: paper and publisher pages blocked, no numbers or direction of the Meyda comparison found; benchmark harness repo found (MTG/essentia.js-benchmarks) but it publishes no results and its node runner feeds undecoded WAV bytes and runs all suites concurrently. Notable as a peer-reviewed, widely used library (870 stars), so kept rather than rejected; retier candidate if the TISMIR PDF becomes reachable.

tier_reason: First-party README table (8000 digits of pi, Node.js v16.14, 'Intel Kaby Lake desktop CPU') matches the record; benchmark code is public (benchmark/calcpi.js) and the current build flags are in binding/*/Dockerfile, but the CPU model is not given and the measured build's toolchain is not stated, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README (8000 digits of pi, same series in every row, Node.js v16.14): JS BigInt 129 ms (1x); gmp-wasm Integer() high-level wrapper 88 ms (1.47x); with delayed deallocation 78 ms (1.65x); MPZ low-level functions 53 ms (2.43x); big-integer 1.6.51 129 ms (1x); decimal.js 10.3.1 443 ms (0.29x). Float series: Float() wrapper 175 ms (0.74x, slower than BigInt), delayed deallocation 169 ms (0.76x), MPFR low-level 118 ms (1.09x), decimal.js float 785 ms (0.16x). The rows Float(1).atan().mul(4) 0.6 ms '215x' and Float('0.5').asin().mul(6) 17 ms '7.59x' are relative to the 129 ms BigInt series (129/0.6 and 129/17, derived from page data) but swap the series for MPFR's built-in atan/asin, so they measure a different algorithm, not the same work.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Current build (v1.3.x): Emscripten emsdk 3.1.58 via binding/gmp/Dockerfile and binding/src/Dockerfile; GMP 6.3.0 with generic C mpn (MPN_PATH=generic, -DNO_ASM), CFLAGS '-O3 -Oz -fno-rtti -fno-exceptions -msimd128 -msse2' (the later -Oz wins, so size-optimized); bindings '-O3 -Oz -flto'. The README numbers were measured on Node.js v16.14 and probably predate the 1.3.0 (2024-07-06) GMP/Emscripten update, so the measured build's flags are not stated.
corrections.caveats: First-party; CPU model not given (only 'Intel Kaby Lake desktop CPU'). The README table appears older than the current benchmark/calcpi.js, which also runs mpzjs, ExactNumber and 'stepwise' solvers absent from the table, and CHANGELOG 1.3.0 updated GMP to 6.3.0, MPFR to 4.2.1 and Emscripten after the Node 16 era. The 215x and 7.59x rows compare MPFR's atan/asin against the BigInt series (different algorithms). The high-level Float wrapper is slower than BigInt (0.74x); only the integer paths and MPFR low-level calls win. Harness is sound otherwise: 5 warm-ups, 4 timed rounds averaged, every result checked against 8000 reference pi digits (the sleep() between rounds is not awaited, so there is no pause). GMP is built size-optimized (-Oz) with generic C limbs and no assembly. Node 16 is old; last commit 2024-07-07.

notes: README numbers confirmed against the record; C stands. Shortcomings: no CPU model, measured build predates current flags, 215x/7.59x rows are an algorithm swap (MPFR atan/asin vs BigInt series), high-level Float wrapper slower than BigInt.
